The Independent — datePublished and dateModified both 2026-10-25T16:11:23Z = 16:11 GMT Sun 25 Oct. Retrieved by curl at 17:35 GMT.

HEADLINE SENSE: Rayner confirms nothing is off the table on Brexit; pro-EU groups put a growth cost on Brexit ahead of Wednesday's Budget.

THE FORUM — THIS IS WHERE THE INDEPENDENT AND THE GUARDIAN DIVERGE
"Ms Rayner was challenged by Laura Kuenssberg on her Sunday morning BBC One show about the prime minister's comment to voters in Makerfield when he fought the by-election there in June that 'now is not the time' to reopen the Brexit debate."
The Guardian attributes Rayner's "just pragmatism" line to Sky News. The Independent places the exchange on BBC One's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg. Both carry the same "can't take anything off the table" formulation, so she may have given both; the forum is not settled by these two reports alone.

RAYNER'S WORDS AS THE INDEPENDENT HAS THEM
"The prime minister is clear that you can't take anything off the table when you're having a conversation. But the prime minister is not saying we're going back to where we were in 2016. He's saying we've got to be pragmatic to get the best deal for Britain and he wants to have the conversation."
To Kuenssberg: "I want to see the best deal for the people of my constituency and for Britain." / "We haven't got the best deal at the moment because we've seen exports reduced by 20 per cent, we've seen the red tape and the friction that has meant that a lot of our businesses are not able to trade in the way that they would like with our biggest trading partners." / "So, I would like us to have an honest conversation about what the trade-offs could be and then put that to the people at a general election."
Note the last clause: she explicitly routes any change through a general election, which matches the standing manifesto red lines.

WHAT THE INDEPENDENT ADDS
Burnham's interview was with The Sunday Times. He said he wanted a "very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this".
"Mr Burnham has committed to the red lines set out in Labour's 2024 manifesto, meaning any change in the relationship would have to wait until after an election."
"The prime minister will meet EU chiefs, including European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen, in Brussels on 20 November."
Stella Creasy, chair of the Labour Movement for Europe, in a slightly fuller version than the Guardian's: "The prime minister is right - the UK is long overdue for a grown-up conversation about what EU freedom of movement actually means to our supply chains and for jobs for British citizens. If we want to negotiate our future with Europe, we need to do so on facts, not fiction."

CAMPAIGN-GROUP NUMBERS — ADVOCACY, NOT OFFICIAL DATA. HANDLE WITH CARE.
European Movement UK: the UK has missed out on between £180bn and £240bn of growth since leaving the EU in 2020, equivalent to £30bn-£40bn a year. Derived by applying a Goldman Sachs / National Bureau of Economic Research estimate of a 6-8 per cent growth shortfall to the OBR's figure of £3.043 trillion for the size of the 2026/27 UK economy.
Best for Britain: an annual tax receipts shortfall of about £40bn; rejoining would boost growth by "at least £92bn".
Neither European Movement UK nor Best for Britain is on the approved-sources list. The OBR and the NBER are. If any of these numbers is used it must be labelled as a campaign-group estimate.
